utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated. May we please hear the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the appearances for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, assisted by Ruth Karper, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. And Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Branko Lukic, Mr. John Ostojic, assisted by Mr. Danilo Cirkovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Due to the fact that we have, as I mentioned last week, to continue as scheduled, I have to come back to three points which have to be decided in the near future. First of all, we still need to reflect on the question of authenticity of some documents. We had already a list of documents, first those carrying a signature by whomsoever, and the intention is by the Chamber to order a graphological expertise by handwriting expert, and it has to be considered and discussed in how far it can be helpful to have, in addition, a forensic writing expert on the documents before us. Those documents bearing no signature at all, here we have to find out whether or not the documents before us are written by a typewriting machine or by a printer and, without doubt, an expert can come to some conclusions whether or not the documents were prepared by the same typewriting machine or by the same printer when it was done by computer. So therefore, the question is ripe, and as we sometimes already stated, this takes time. And therefore, we invite the parties hereby to address this issue no later than next Monday. Then the Chamber will decide. Second, having had some experiences, to put it neutral, with the calculation of the expected time for at least the examination-in-chief, we would ask the OTP to prepare us -- to prepare for us a realistic calculation of the expected time for examination-in-chief for all the witnesses still to come, in order to have ourselves a realistic basis for the schedule, the schedule that is necessary for September, October, November. And, finally, the kind request goes to proofing notes and exhibit numbers of the witness to come tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Your Honour means Charles McLeod, there are no proofing notes. And can I tell Your Honour now, the only evidence I shall be adducing from him will be the record of his conversation with the accused, plus his conclusions at the end of his visit. And that is based, I think Your Honours have already had the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. Then if there's nothing, then we know. And the estimated time will be?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have said half an hour in chief, but because of the reading of the document into the record, I'll allow an hour. Can I just remind Your Honours, he has to leave tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, therefore my question: You start immediately tomorrow, 9.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then examination-in-chief until?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At the latest, 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 10.00. Probably, we then can really finalise until 12.00 or 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just mention before the witness comes back one matter, and that relates to the witness that Your Honours wanted to require to attend for a videolink. He's the gentleman -- I can't remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There are two.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Two, yes, but this is the one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not sure that he's not protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, I'll just stop and say (redacted) full stop, (redacted). And a lady from a mixed marriage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. Yes, it's the Witness G, Your Honour. What we've discovered subsequently is that for him to attend at either Sarajevo or Banja Luka for the videolink would require a five-hour one-way journey for him in a car, in considerable heat as it now is in Bosnia. As Your Honour knows, the reason that we asked for him to be Rule 92 is that he has a heart condition, and we're wondering whether Your Honours might reconsider in the light of that whether or not you still require him to give evidence through videolink. That's all; we're just raising it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As things have changed, probably we have to come back to even third solutions. And what about the other witness to be expected?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as I know, there's no real problem with the other witness. We're starting to make arrangements for the videolink. We were unaware at the time -- he, when he agreed to it, thought that it was going to be in the place that he lives. And it can't be, we don't think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Good. Then may we start with the cross-examination. And I wonder if it wouldn't be in the interest of all the participants to continue with this witness until 11.40, and then have a break of half an hour. This would allow us to proceed only with one break this morning. Fine. Okay. Then the witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated. As there was a really prolonged weekend in between, I regard it as necessary to recall that also the upcoming questions has to be answered in a way that you don't run into any kind of problems as to the fact that you are still under the solemn declaration. Then, the examination --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, before you go on, Ms. Karper has reminded me, in our discussions, I think we may have identified the witness. I wonder if you could just order it to be redacted from the transcript. He is the subject of protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Probably there were two letters or even three letters too many. They may please be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it is a problem. That's the problem. With the initial, plus where he is. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before we continue, would Your Honours allow me to address you, please. During the several previous days during the trial here at the Tribunal, several documents have been tendered into evidence bearing my name and surname: the documents which were signed and stamped by Mr. Vojo Kupresanin, the President of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. The documents in question were actually photocopies, that is, the photocopies have been provided to the Court. You asked about one of the documents, and she said that the original was with me. At that moment, I did not -- could not remember it. The Prosecutor probably had better information or could remember the issue. I looked through the documents that I have and I've found the original of the document. At that moment last week, I couldn't remember the fact that I possessed the original. But in the meantime, I have managed to find it and, Your Honours, I hereby would like to submit this original to you so that you have it as part of your file. But I would like to have a photocopy of this document. I don't know what number it would be given in this case, but I believe that the relevant authorities will decide on it. So I'm hereby giving you the original document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could the usher, please, present it first to the Defence. And could the registry please find out what was the document number. 110, 15, there in the neighbourhood. If it then could be shown to us. I think the Prosecutor has seen the document? Not yet. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we haven't. Obviously, we can't talk to Mr. Sejmenovic, and we're not sure what document he's talking about at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Can it be agreed that we take the document under the number we have with an additional "-1," B-1, and may, please, the Prosecutor prepare a photocopy, another photocopy, of this document for the witness before us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just -- it's S153. Is Your Honour asking us to take the original and make it a court exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The original --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you. The original as a court exhibit, and then a photocopy to be provided as requested for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If it becomes a court exhibit, I'm not sure how the witness will ever get it back again. I don't think he will. It will just be filed with the Court. And whether Your Honours having seen the original require it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: My understanding was that the witness would be -- I think it would be enough for him to have a photocopy only. This was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could just confirm that he understands that, that he won't get the original back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Because I heard -- I understood that the original was necessary for the purposes of credibility. So I am willing to give this document, the original one, to the Court, and only keep a photocopy of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm told, Your Honour, it's S153.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this original document is then admitted into evidence, if there is no objection, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There is no objection, Your Honour, just that we can't authenticate the signature, but I would like the opportunity to ask the witness a couple questions on this very document before the original is taken away for photocopying, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But not to forget, admitted into evidence as S153 B-1. And then may the usher please give the original once again to the witness before it's later on copied. So I think now we can start.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a series of questions today, but first I'd like to, with respect to the exhibit that you've just tendered this morning to us, ask you a couple of questions. So if the usher would be kind enough to give you the original back.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to the document that's before you, can you just generally identify the document, what is it and what is the date that it bears on the document?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document bears the date the 19th of August, 1992. The title of the document, that is, the heading is: "The Serbian Republic, the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, Banja Luka." This is a copy which was signed and stamped by the President of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. The purpose of the document was to enable me to travel to the centre of the Banja Luka town pursuant to an invitation of the relevant authorities and to have the required interviews or conversations. So in order for me to be able to pass through the military checkpoints, I was given this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Further, with respect to that document, to the best of your opinion, does it bear an original signature or does it at the very least have an original ink on it with respect to the signature?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an original, the original that I was personally given. It was compiled and stamped in the office of the President of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and it was Mr. Kupresanin, the president of the region himself, who gave this document to me. He was the one who signed the document and stamped it. As for the ink or the colour of the pencil, I don't know. I wasn't looking at it. But the document is authentic and original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not debating that, with you, sir. But look at the ink. What colour is the ink of the signature: blue, black, red?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ink is blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right, right. And that blue ink also bears a blue stamp, correct? And therefore it's your conclusion, because it has a original signature with the original colour of the ink that's reflected on that document with a stamp over that signature, to you, it's an original document. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the reason why I consider it to be an original. This is an original because I was personally given this document by him. It was impossible for him to give me a forgery at the time. He said: "I'm now going to write a certificate for you which you will have to carry on you when passing through the checkpoints." Several minutes later, the certificate was written out. He signed it and stamped it, and he gave it to me personally for my personal use.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us, Mr. Sejmenovic -- and I understand that. My point is, can you share with us, when you were the deputy in the chamber of the municipalities for the Prijedor Municipality, whether the stamp would generally accompany the original signature? Do you know if it would or not?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, let me describe for you a general principle which I believe is applicable in your country as well. If someone holds an office, then it is usually the secretaries who type out various forms of documents for that person. Chiefs of these offices are in charge of signing these documents, and then placing a stamp on it. That is a perfectly normal procedure in respect of the majority of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I couldn't agree with you more, Mr. Sejmenovic. So is it fair to say, sir, that if a document has a photocopy of a signature but bears on top of that an original stamp, it is less authentic, less credible, and obviously not signed or stamped contemporaneously with the date that it bears on the document, unlike this document which clearly has the original stamp and the original signature? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I really don't know what you're talking about. I'm really not competent to answer this type of questions. It really falls outside my scope of interest. You're trying to argue the original character of the document that I was given on the spot. I will tell you once again how it happened. I was taken to the office of Mr. Kupresanin. He said: "We are going to issue a certificate in your name." He was the one who wrote the certificate. He signed it. He stamped it. And it was with this document that I was taken to Bosanska Vrbanja. So the certificate which I was personally given by him, which he personally signed and stamped, constitute an original for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Again, as I said, I don't debate that with you, nor am I arguing with you. I agree with you. My point is, while you were a member of the republic assembly, did you ever have an occasion to see a document that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. had your signature, but a photocopy of that signature, and subsequently it bore an original stamp in the blue ink that you see there? Have you ever experienced that in the time that you were a member of the republic assembly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the issue of authenticating originals? That is, of authenticating photocopies of original documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why don't we move on to another subject? I think I've exhausted your understanding of the original. And I just wanted for the record to make clear that that document that we have, S153-1, actually bears a blue ink signature and a blue ink stamp. In any event, thank you, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you could be kind enough to return that original to the usher. Sir, at the end of the session last week Thursday, we started to discuss arms, weapons, and armaments, and whether the SDA members solicited funds and/or money to those arms for the Bosnian Muslims -- for the Bosnian Muslim population in Prijedor before April of 1992. You stated, if you remember, in the last five or so minutes of your testimony, that in fact, "Bosnian Muslims in 1992 were able to purchase weapons from a large number of Serbs, Serbs from Omarska, Serbs from Prijedor, and even some Serbs from the barracks." My question to you, sir: In addition to those persons that you've identified, were the Bosnian Muslims prior to April and May of 1992 able to purchase weapons from any Croats?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When answering your question, I wasn't talking about Bosnian Muslims but about people who lived in Kozarac. What I know or, rather, what I heard from people, because I'm not an eyewitness to any sale or purchase of weapons, this was just hearsay that I heard. I heard that some Serbs from Omarska were selling weapons and that one could buy weapons from them. I also heard that similar things were happening in the town of Prijedor and that even some people from the barracks were doing this. I repeat, I was not an eyewitness to any such transaction, nor was this fact ever debated in the party or in the Territorial Defence. This is something we simply heard about and something that was done by individuals, and the number of such cases was purely symbolic. I, therefore, limit this to the area of Kozarac and Prijedor and to the general sort of information I had about this. And this is all I can say on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So did they or did they not, the people from Kozarac or the people from Prijedor, namely, the Bosnian Muslims, were they able to purchase arms from Croats?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of Kozarac, there were very, very few Croats, almost none. There may have been a dozen families or so. The areas inhabited by Croats were on the other end of the Prijedor Municipality, in the area of Ljubija and on towards the mountains. What went on there, I don't know. And this was never something we discussed officially. So I did not get any information about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you did not have any first-hand or direct information and you certainly didn't have any second-hand information in connection with the purchase of arms by Bosnian Muslims in the Kozara area from any Croats. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the Croats in the municipality of Prijedor were in the same situation as the Bosnian Muslims. They shared the same fate. Their houses were burned and they were taken to camps just like the Bosniak Muslims. When the Serbs took over power, the Croats did not share power, so they had the same problem as the Muslims. And now you're asking us whether we could rely on them because, according to you, they had weapons and were even able to sell them. Let me repeat, we shared the same fate because we were not Serbs and we were in the same situation as the rest of the non-Serbian population. That is why I doubt your theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's not a theory, sir. So is your answer, no, the Bosnian Muslims did not obtain arms or weapons from Croats?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that such a thing was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your direct response. With respect to the Kozara police department and police station, prior to April of 1992, sir, was it comprised of mostly the residents in the Kozarac area who were of the ethnic Muslim group?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that there were also members of other ethnic groups, according to the proportion they had in the population. I can't tell you exactly what the composition was because that wasn't something I was interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, you told us in Kozarac there were very few, maybe ten or so homes that were Croatian. Do you know of any of those Croats who were members of the Kozarac police station or police department prior to May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that the number of Croats in the area of Kozarac was some ten or so families. The numbers were not large. And let me repeat, I do not know what the ethnic breakdown of the police force was. There may have been some individuals who were not Bosniak Muslims but the composition reflected the composition of the population. I know this principle was respected until the last moment, of course, if the people so wished. But I can't answer your question with any precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you name one Serb who was a member of the Kozarac police station prior to April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. It's possible that there were some, but I can't remember any.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of the population in Kozarac, the area that we've talked about, Kozarac, what was the percentage of Muslim residents, 97, 99 per cent?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vast majority or the absolute majority. There was a small percentage of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many people were members of this Kozarac police force or police department in April or before April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know either before or after April. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From November 1990, sir, when you took office as a member of the chamber of municipalities from Prijedor, did you have any idea of what the number of members were in the Kozarac police force?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know. Why would I know? What member of parliament of a country knows how many policemen there are, not even in a municipality but in a local commune, in the smallest unit of self-government? How would I know? There were 40 or 36 such local communes in Prijedor. How would I know how many policemen there were in each? It was simply not the subject matter I dealt with. Had I been the chief of police, I would probably have known this, but I wasn't so I don't know. I don't know this information either before or during the war. It was not part of my job and it was not one of the issues it was my duty to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Speaking of those duties, did the chief of police have to report to you as a member of the republic assembly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally and legally, no one in the municipality of Prijedor was subordinate to me. My post was such that I could influence the bills or the proposals for changing regulations at the republic level.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you know how many reserve police officers were members of the Kozarac police force prior to April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't have this information. Everything I said in answer to your previous answer also refers to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, with respect to that, I have a follow-up question, unfortunately. That is, do you know, sir, how many weapons the members of the police force, the regular members of the police force of the Kozarac police department, as well as the reserve policemen, how many weapons did they have prior to April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. I repeat: I don't know. Because I did not analyse this information, nor was it my duty to deal with it. This was at the local level, and you can ask the chief of police there that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, with respect to the issue of weapons, is it true that the young men who were watching and who were on duty in the vicinity of your home, which was near the sentry posts toward the railroad tracks, near the fish ponds, was it true that, in fact, they had bottles of petrol with rags in them, which as we commonly referred to as the Molotov cocktail, and that they used those weapons as a defence mechanism on those checkpoints right near your town? True or false?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is an erroneous interpretation of information I gave previously. I can repeat: I know about at least one case, and there may have been many such cases. The case I know about, I can describe again in detail and I can draw, I can make a sketch of the exact position where that young man was. And of course, I think it's useful for me to say that no one in the Trnopolje local commune in the Territorial Defence knew how to make a Molotov cocktail. And this young man poured a litre of petrol into a bottle from his car tank, and with this litre of petrol, he kept guard at the place designated for him by the Territorial Defence in case they were attacked, in case a tank came along. Then he would aim the bottle of petrol at the tank. I know that there were four persons on that spot, and not a single one of them had any weapons. All they had was that bottle of petrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that clarification. But let me just, so that we're clear on this point, direct your attention to your testimony on May 24th, 1996, page 928, specifically, lines 3 through 9, or 3 through 11 is what I'm going to focus on. At that time, Mr. Sejmenovic, you gave testimony and your answer is a little lengthy here, so I'm just going to focus on that part. If the Court would like me to read the entire answer, I can, but it's rather lengthy. I'd just like to focus on line 3. On line 3, page 928 of your May 1996 testimony, you state, among other things: "For instance, I remember that in the vicinity of the house where I lived that several sentry posts towards the railway tracks and fish farms, that was the direction from which we expected the infantry attack might be launched. The sentries were lads, were young men, who were not armed with anything. They did not have any rifles. Most of them, not even those pistols. But they would have a bottle of petrol with a rag in it, with a piece of cloth in it. And that was the only thing they had with them to spend on duty, to spend on guard through the night. They did not even know how to make it, what you call it, Molotov cocktail. They simply poured the petrol from the car into bottles. That was how they did it. There was simply no time, no weaponry, no skilled people, professionals, army officers who could organise it, unfortunately." Now, that testimony seems to indicate, at least to me, sir, respectfully, that there was more than one person and that there was more than one bottle which was filled with fuel or petrol which was used as a weapon at this checkpoint near your home by the railway tracks near the fish farms.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to respond to that. You said that, in my previous statement, I said they made Molotov cocktails. I denied this because there was simply no one who knew how to make such a thing. Secondly, in response to your question, I told you I saw one person with a bottle. I know there were several such persons, and I heard that they were at several sentry posts who had to do this, but they did not really know how to make home-made bombs. So I repeat, this is correct, and I can repeat it again. But with my own eyes, I saw the son of one of my neighbours holding this bottle.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to the weapons that we discussed that are reflected in the list of the TO mobilisation that we talked about yesterday, and some of which we discussed today, you mentioned also last Thursday the issue of blacksmiths. Isn't it true, sir, that immediately before the war, you and your group contracted - not contacted but contracted - a few, not just one, but a few blacksmiths in order to manufacture weapons for the Muslim residents and people in the Kozara area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a contract of any kind. Simply, there were several blacksmiths and people asked them whether any one of them knew how to make a weapon, something that could be used with gunpowder. I heard about this on the ground, not at an official meeting. I know that in the village of Kamicani, there was a blacksmith whose name I think was Besim, and I know he made several old-fashioned rifles or pistols, something that looks like a pistol. I know that they tried to make weapons, and that hand-made weapons were later confiscated by the Serbian authorities who later spoke of the manufacture of weapons. But this was not organised. There were not enough blacksmiths. This is a rather rare trade. There were few of them left. I personally know of two blacksmiths on an area with 25.000 inhabitants. There may have been three or four of them, but not more. Of the two I know, I know that one did not know how to make weapons, and he simply didn't succeed in this. I think the other one, whose name I think was Besim, although I'm not sure, managed to produce two or three weapons. And people thought they could shoot out of those weapons if there was a necessity to defend the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in addition to those blacksmiths, sir, in fact, there were other people who did some metal processing, who also manufactured their own weapons. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I'm only telling you about what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to the testimony that you gave in the trial on July 13th, 1998, specifically, page 503. Again, your answer is somewhat lengthy at that time but I'll read the section starting on line 2 of page 503, if I may. Thank you. Line 2, page 503: "Immediately before the war, since there was no other solution available, we contracted a few blacksmiths. We wanted them to make some kind of home-made pistols, guns, with metal tubes, because people were afraid and there weren't enough weapons. And that was a way for the people to try to obtain some kind of weapons to arm themselves and to defend themselves. And we managed to produce some of those guns, and some other people who did some metal processing, they also manufactured their own weapons." In 1998, sir, it seems that not only were blacksmiths contracted, they produced weapons for the residents of Kozarac, but also individuals who were in the metal processing expertise also produced weapons. Is it your testimony today that the metal processing people that you mentioned in 1998 did not manufacture their own guns? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking of 1998? That's a mistake. We're talking of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Pardon me for interrupting you. The reference to 1998 was your testimony in the Kovacevic case which was in July of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, okay. Yes, now I understand. I apologise. Let me repeat: I knew of the blacksmith Besim in Kamicani who produced several improvised weapons. That's the first thing. Secondly, I know that some blacksmiths did not know how to do this. For example, Meho Hodzic, who was a neighbourhood of mine and who was a blacksmith, didn't know how to do this. I also heard that some people who were not blacksmiths manufactured their own weapons, people who were metal workers, who knew how to handle metal. I heard about this also. And in the end, for the first time at this Tribunal, I saw lists of weapons where I saw hand-made weapons listed. And then it became clear to me that the information I had only heard but I had no personal knowledge of this, I realised that some people who were not blacksmiths had managed to produce weapons. Let me repeat: Anyone who could find any means of preparing for defence to prevent a massacre tried to do so, either by making a weapon or using a bottle of petrol or improvising some sort of weapon. This was simply a process of self-defence which took its course. We are speaking of the period just before the war, when the Serbs had already taken over power in Prijedor with the army and had reinforced their positions around Kozarac, and people were trying to do what they could, without any success. On the other side, you had the most up-to-date weapons and guns, and on this side you had people with bottles of petrol and handmade guns who were given the worst possible sort of ultimatum, and claims were being made that they were armed to the teeth. Let me summarise: The Territorial Defence, or rather the command of the Territorial Defence in Kozarac, did not recruit blacksmiths or metal workers. The Territorial Defence in Kozarac did its job. Certain individuals tried to, at least, improvise a weapon if they could, by any means. And let me repeat: I know of a specific case where a blacksmith in Kamicani produced several weapons. I know some blacksmiths did not do this. I know that some men managed to produce their own weapons. How? I don't know. I assume that they knew how to work with metal or they couldn't have done it. So they knew how to process metal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think I understand your testimony. But can you just clarify this for me, Mr. Sejmenovic: Were you a member of the command of the Territorial Defence in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How do you know then, not being a member, not actively participating in the Territorial Defence, not even, according to your testimony, having any weapon or arm, how do you know, sir, if the command of the Territorial Defence did or did not contact and contract these other blacksmiths? How would you know?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I knew about the local Territorial Defence in my local commune. I know all the important orders that arrived. So if this had been the case, I would have said so. It's in my interest to tell the truth, to say everything that happened. It's in all of our interest. I know that in the village of Garibi, for example, a young man who was 19 years old managed to make a weapon by himself. And he thought it was a weapon. He managed to put a bullet in it and to prepare it for use. He was not a blacksmith. He was not a metal worker, but he managed to do it. I also know that the local Territorial Defence had a blacksmith, Meho Hodzic, but they never, ever said to him: "Meho, from now on you are going to produce weapons." I would have known this if it had happened. If they had received any such order, they would certainly have passed it on to Mr. Meho Hodzic. So I am speaking of the local community where I lived. And finally people came to me and asked me: "Is there anyone who knows how to make weapons? Why is the Territorial Defence not organising something? We should try and do something." Therefore, as for the command of the Territorial Defence, I don't know. But I know that they issued orders to the local Territorial Defence units and that the local unit never received such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I know your testimony in connection with the Kozarac police station and police department, both the regular police officers and the reserve, that you do not know how many weapons they had prior to April of 1992. Do you know, sir, who the individual was who was in charge of that police station prior to April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who it was. But I do know that there was a gentleman called Osman who went to negotiate in Prijedor on behalf of the police station. Whether he was a chief, he may have been, but I'm not sure. I don't remember very well. Osman, who people called Osmaj [phoen], usually, whether that was his post before, I don't know whether he was formerly the chief of police. I don't know. He may have been. I can't say with any certainty whether he was or was not. But I do know that he went to Prijedor to talk with the Crisis Staff and the Serbian authorities on behalf of the police. And I know that he never came back from those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When were those negotiations in terms of a time reference? Was it before or after April 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just before the attack on Kozarac, perhaps a day before. According to some information, he had already been to Prijedor once to negotiate and come back. And then when he went there the second time, he never came back, according to some information. But all I know for sure is that he did go, and perhaps there are people who were still alive whom you can ask about the details of these contacts as far as the police and Territorial Defence are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: From the time of November 1990 up until April of 1992, when the late Mr. Cehajic was president of the Municipal Assembly, did he have any competencies or rights to either control, command, or punish members of the Kozarac police department, or direct them as to where they should go, what they should be doing, and when they should be doing it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the municipality who held the highest ranking post in the municipality could contact the members of the municipal government directly. He had the competency of replacing the president of the municipal government. He also had the power to evaluate the work of the ministers of the municipal government. Of course, his basic job was legislative and he had to convene the assembly and take care that laws were implemented. In cases of emergency - in cases of emergency, I repeat - he became the chief of a body which was set up under emergency situations, and it was called the National Defence Council. And then he had the highest competencies and powers to rule directly, I think. Yes. He had direct authority to influence the chiefs of particular services at lower levels. That's what I know, and those are general facts. Anyone who took any part in government would know that. As for the actual legislation dealing with his competencies and powers, well, you can have a look at those laws and legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, quite frankly, I have. Do you, as you sit here, being a member of the legislative republic assembly, recall specifically that competencies as you've just alleged and asserted with respect to the local president of the Municipal Assembly, is it your position that they exist in writing or existed at that time?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the documents in writing, the competencies of the National Defence Council were provided for in relevant documents, and it is the president of the municipality who is, by virtue of his office, the chief of that body. In accordance with pre-war laws which were very specific, all of these functions were stipulated and detailed. But I cannot tell you much about how it actually functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the National Defence Council existed while the time Mr. Cehajic was president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure. I think that it was on these -- the insistence of the Yugoslav People's Army, that is, Mr. Arsic in particular, and the SDS, as far as I can recall, that talks were conducted and that the body -- that this body was established. At least, attempts were made to establish such a body. Whether any sessions were held and how many, whether anything was discussed and what, I don't know. I don't know because I was not a member of this council.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the members of the council were?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By virtue of their offices, as far as I can remember, the members of the council were the president of the municipality, the president of the municipal government, the minister, that is, the chief of police, chief of Territorial Defence as well, I believe, a representative of the military if it happened to be located in the area, that is, the JNA, and possibly someone else. I would probably need some time to think and I will be able to give you a more precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to your participation and membership in the republic assembly as a member of the chamber of municipalities in Prijedor, can you tell us or describe for us the hierarchial structure of the various police stations that existed in the Prijedor municipality from November of 1990 through April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know very little about it, I must admit. I know that there was a Ministry of the Interior which existed at the level of the state, that the person in charge was the Minister of the Interior, who reported to the Prime Minister, the president of the government, or to the assembly or the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina upon their invitation. His department, that is, the Ministry of the Interior, was organised in such a way that it had regional police centres and local police centres, that is, at the level of the municipalities. And even further below, at the level of larger local communes or associations of local communes, that would be the general structure of this ministry, and that's what I know about. But as for the details, I really cannot tell you much. Also, practically speaking, I did not have a duty to analyse these structures in depth. I also know that it was divided into the sector of public security and the sector or department of state security, and the traffic department, that is, the traffic safety sector, the traffic control. I don't know what exactly this department was called. The traffic police, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For purposes of clarity, when you mention on line 9 of today's transcript, "Ministry of the Interior which existed at the level of the state," that would be, in your mind, the republic level or the federal level?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am referring to the republic level.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When you say that the person in charge was the Minister of the Interior who reported to the prime minister, the prime minister of the republic level, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He reported to the prime minister at the level of the republic. We had the corresponding type of structure and authority at the local level, as far as local competencies are concerned. The minister of the interior -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When you say the Minister of the Interior was in this hierarchical structure that you described, he also responded or was obligated to report to the president of the government, again, you mean the president or the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and not the president of any local government of the 109 municipalities, correct? It was that he reported to, solely and exclusively, to the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Minister of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina is a member of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As such, he is directly subordinated to the prime minister. And I repeat: If necessary, or if invited to do so, he was also obliged to report to the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and also to inform the presidency and the assembly of BH about his activities. As for the local level, local problems and the local level of police functioning, a very similar structure and very similar hierarchical relations existed, that is the chief of police was directly responsible to the president of the Executive Board, but he was also obligated to report to the president of the municipality on his activities, which was done in practice, at least in respect of major issues that he was supposed to deal with. Again, if need arose, or if invited, he would also report to the Municipal Assembly on his activities. I'm telling you about this general insight that I have in this structure. As for the legal specificities of the issue, I do not feel competent to speak about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And due -- is it your testimony that there is some document or statute which establishes this local hierarchy that you just described at the municipal level? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I don't know. I am not able to speak about statutory regulations. I'm telling you about the practice which could be observed in every municipality. A parallel structure existed at the local municipal level and at the republic level. You can ask me hundreds of questions regarding the relevant statutory provisions but I really do not feel competent to tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So the gentleman Hasan Talundzic, do you know him, correct? Or you knew him, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Hasan Talundzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was he obligated, at least according to you, to report to both Mr. Cehajic and Dr. Kovacevic from the period of November 1990 to April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, the direct --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes or no, was he obligated according to your testimony just now --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me try to change the subject for a moment, sir, if you permit me. Do you know a gentleman by the name of Evledin Rizvanovic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the person by the name Evledin Rizvan, a gentleman from Prijedor, from the Puharska neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We're talking about the same individual. I have it as "Rizvanovic" but nevertheless, was this gentleman you're referring to a member of the Crisis Staff on or about April and May of 1992? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I do not know that a Kozarac Crisis Staff was ever established, at least formally speaking. Second, I know the person by the name of Evledin Risvan from Puharska. I don't know a person by that name as a resident of Kozarac, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, a person by the name of Ismet Kurtovic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman by the name of Esad Alisic, who was a reserve captain and who purportedly was involved in arming the Muslims in the Kozara area in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, what did you say his name was?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Esad Alisic.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've heard the name and the surname, but I don't know the person by the name of Esad Alisic. There's quite a few individuals by the surname of Alisic. It sounds like a name of a Prijedor or Kozarac resident.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman or person by the name of Jusuf Ramic, who was chief of the Crisis Staff from April 25th, 1992, and commander of the regional Territorial Defence headquarters from the 21st of May, 1992? Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me, with the Court's permission, show you a document that we're going to ask be marked as the next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Provisional D12.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I can have the usher tender the first copy, because it has some markings on it, to the OTP, and then the balance, one to the witness and then to the Court, please. Just so the record is clear, this was included in our May 2002 binder, just so that when we go back to retrieve it, we'll remember where to look for it. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I just mention, Your Honours, this was disclosed to the Defence. And if Your Honours look at the first page of the English translation, which it's not even a translation, it's a summary, it contains a translator's note. Your Honour, it has got nothing to do with the document. It was an internal note. It shouldn't have been disclosed in that form, but it has been disclosed, but it has nothing whatsoever to do with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I most definitely disagree with counsel on this point. It's clear why they object to the translator's note, but I think it defies logic why the entire document of in excess of 250 pages was not translated in the English language, why we only received excerpts of that document, and I would like, if permitted, to ask this witness what his thoughts are on that document, specifically since the OTP's very own translator believes that the main value with this document lies in the description of how the Muslim Territorial Defence was organised. Respectfully for the Court, I see it says "TO" on the English trans, but that's "obrana" for "defence." I think that's what it means. In addition, there are some concrete issues within the summary that we have that I would like to ask this witness, having been in the Kozarac area and specifically knowing some of these individuals, and I think that we can and should be permitted to put this document to the witness and obtain his position or opinion on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not objecting to that. I'm not objecting to -- I'm merely pointing out that the translator's note is internal, is personal. I don't know who the translator was. And therefore, it can't be, as it were, taken as a statement of fact or whatever. So Mr. Ostojic is perfectly able to put the summary if he wants to, to the witness, but the translator's note is not of any evidential value, we submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we have to live with this, as it is normally international custom, a translated document should bear the signature of the translator and stamp. But here, we have additional translator's notice, and that is open also for our French speaking colleagues, it reads: "This is an account of personal experience, detailed and thorough, but does not contain many facts. There are very few dates in the text. I think that the main value lies in the description of how the Muslim TO was organised. The statement seems unbiased and is equally critical of Muslims and Serbs. It is not clear what is hearsay and what the witness experienced." And then a line, and then "instruction for use," and I don't know whether here already starts the document, but probably the witness can tell us on the basis of the document before him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If there are no copies for the interpreters, can the original be -- or the translation be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Does the Defence have another copy for the booth?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Regretfully, we don't. And the original transcript, just so that we have a clear record, of the document that we're referring to was received by us, I believe, on this past Saturday. And if I can just enter the ERN number, which starts with 00798786 and proceeds approximately 237 pages and ends at 00799030.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: My understanding is that you want to tender only the pages we have available in B/C/S ending with page 184. This is the ERN number 977 at the end. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At this time, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we can't see the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I received the document in the very manner in which I photocopied it. So I have the document which was subsequently provided to us, which has the first page which I believe accurately is translated, which is the first page of our document bearing the ERN number L0001604. And I'd be happy to tender that to the Court for its review.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just ask, the copy I have been given has all sorts of markings on the translation. Why is that? Do Your Honours have markings? I've got highlight, I've got sort of names being in square brackets around them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I hope that the Court doesn't have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We, too, have, and with great interest follow this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's not how it was disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Those are my markings. If I can withdraw that and make the appropriate copy. It was my understanding that we copied the unmarked version, Your Honour. So I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Apparently, it's only names and, yeah, okay. But once again, we have to concentrate. The document never can be the translation. The document can only be the B/C/S document, and apparently the beginning of page 13 it starts, and there is a blanket on the top of the page. Then it continues until page 16, continues with 20, 77, 110, 184. So it's just a compilation of several pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may proceed, since we have approximately ten minutes, maybe we could get through this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I can use this document, understanding the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, it states on this document, I believe, that Evledin Rizvanovic, the individual that you know, as you've told us it states here, according to Mr. Jusuf Ramic, that he was a criminal, pushed forward by the SDA. Being a member of the SDA, do you know if: (a) Mr. Rizvanovici was a criminal; and why was he pushed forward by the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me ask you -- let me answer with two elements in response to your question. First of all, it was not my job to establish who criminals were. Second, at the time the party was developing at the local level and at the time of the creation of other political parties, generally speaking, a number of people took up certain positions, certain functions, which was a perfectly natural process at that time. So neither myself nor the president of the initiative committee dealt with criminal records of various individuals. We knew that we should not allow for a well-known criminal, and in respect of whom we had relevant information, to become appointed or elected to a specific position. The SDA had several thousand of members at that time. We were trying to establish it without the assistance of the relevant social structures at the time, and we had no way of checking everything. So these things normally happened at that time. The work of the people was a voluntary one, and it was the case with other parties as well, such as the SDS or HDZ. Only those individuals in respect of whom it was evident that they had criminal record were prevented from running for certain functions. Later on, when it was discovered that some of them -- that certain individuals were -- had criminal record, then steps were taken to remove that person from office. I didn't know anything about Mr. Rizvanovic at the time, if he had a criminal record and if -- well, if that's what you state on the basis of this document, then I can just say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Ismet Kurtovic was in charge of acquiring weapons for the Muslims in the period of April and May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know only about a musician whose name was Ismet Kurtovic. He was a member of the well-known pop band. He lives in Croatia now. As for Ismet Kurtovic from Prijedor, I don't know anything about that person. I don't remember that name, at least at this moment. I will think about it during the break. But I'm sure that I would have known if he had been of any significance in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is there any reason that you know of as to why Mr. Ramic would put down in a 235-plus page report that Ismet Kurtovic was in charge of acquiring weapons for Muslims, why you would think that would be incorrect since you don't know the individual?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. How can he answer that question? He has already said he doesn't know Mr. Ramic. How can he know whether or not what was in the mind of Mr. Ramic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: In this report by Mr. Ramic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, I would like to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sejmenovic. No, I'm kidding, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But please take care that you -- you are here as a witness, and not -- it's indeed not a guessing game. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, immediately below where Ismet Kurtovic's name appears on page 4 of the English transcript, it says specifically: "Provocation by Muslims organised by the SDA." Do you, sir, have any information or knowledge whatsoever what the provocation was and who at the SDA organised it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, sir, let me try to answer the four previous questions. You're asking me about an individual whom I do not know. Had this person been important in this whole process, I would have surely known him. Further, this individual makes mention of a number of other persons whom I had never met. I do not know about the individuals you have just named. While you were talking to Their Honours, I took the opportunity of going through this document and reading the portions of the document. I fully respect the right of the gentleman by the name of Jusuf Ramic to have certain opinions and impressions, however the document here contains some very stupid, preposterous things. He is identifying some 98 intellectuals as members of the party. He's also speaking about the internal boundaries of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time or, as it is stated here, the official of the SDA in Prijedor and the one in Bihac had quarrelled before the war as to the centre of the canton, whether it would be in Prijedor or in Bihac. I mean, this is complete nonsense. I merely wish to emphasise that you are bringing me in a very difficult moral situation. You're asking me to state my opinion about the individuals whom I do not know, and to comment on certain very absurd things. I fully understand the requirements of your job. Of course, I'm perfectly willing to answer your questions, but I specifically emphasise the fact that I am not familiar with these names, except the Evledin Rizvanovic. As for the activities that you mentioned, I must say that the SDA did not dare speak about any provocations at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's true, sir, according to what you're telling us, from April 30th, 1992, all the way through May 21st, 1992, right? Never even discussed provocation, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's not true?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was true throughout that period of time, ever since the setting up of the SDA. If you're talking about provocations, it was the SDA that was provoked. You did not ask me any question about that, nor did Their Honours ask me any such questions. Had they done so, I would have been able to give you an answer. It was us who suffered a number of provocations because we were in a very difficult situation, in particular, with respect of the power, with the force, that we had -- that we were faced with.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand, and we talked about that a little bit. Just to go back to telling us about this individual, I'm certainly, sir, not asking you to pass judgement on any individual here, including Mr. Ramic. But you state that if he was in a position of some influence or power, you would have known him. The author states that he was chief of the Crisis Staff from 25 April, 1992, and the commander of the regional Territorial Defence headquarters from the 21st of May, 1992. Is it your position that you don't know who this person is?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have already told you, I don't know anything about the existence of this Crisis Staff. As the deputy president of the party, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It talks about on a subsequent page, and again, I'm just trying to cover these topics with you, the illegal arm trafficking mainly done by Serbs but also by brothers Enes and Senad Kapetanovic. Did you, sir, know either Enes or Senad Kapetanovic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. These are people from the area of Prijedor, from the villages surrounding Prijedor. I lived in the other end of Prijedor, in the Kozarac area, which is 15 kilometres away from the town of Prijedor. You're asking me about persons who were known locally, and I can honestly say that I know nothing about them. You may go on, of course, but I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: According to Mr. Ramic, it says: "Apparently the Muslim TO acquired a huge amount of weapons." Mr. Ramic, being the chief of the Crisis Staff and commander of the regional TO, would you agree with me, sir, that he is in a better position to determine the amount of weapons, arms, and armaments the Territorial Defence had in April and May of 1992 than yourself?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't want to interrupt again. That depends very much on whether this man is who he says he was. And unless my learned friend knows for a fact that he was who he says he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can't imagine the OTP would give us a document with its very own comments that states that the statement seems unbiased and is equally critical of the Muslims and Serbs, and now will tell us that it may or may not be fraudulent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the difficulty about -- that's what I meant. I don't know who this translator is. I don't know how he or she came to make the comments. That's why I'm saying it's not something that we would respectfully submit the Court or indeed the Defence can take into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we shouldn't dispute too much about this. I would appreciate if we could have, after the break, the first page of the entire document and, of course, the last page, to find out whether there is a signature or whatsoever. And -- yes. In English, the cover page reads: "Report received and signed for by the military attache, BH Senad Kubat."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Does the witness know this person, Senad Kubat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do know Senad Kubat. He was in the local SDA in Bosanska Gradiska, and he held a post there. Later on, during the war, he worked at the consulate of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb for a brief time, and then he was dismissed from that job. He was dismissed because he had certain characteristics that were incompatible with work in the diplomatic service.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's come back after the break to the question of the authenticity of the underlying document. And the trial stands adjourned until 10 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Did the parties agree, if I may ask, what we have before us, a document or a fragment or whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I didn't realise Your Honour was asking us to agree. It's a summary of what's in the document, translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. A summary, but not of that what follows in B/C/S. In B/C/S, therefore, are some pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. And therefore, it is difficult to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we'll try to clarify it if I may, Your Honour. As the chronology was, the document that we received in a May 2002 binder included the very pages and exhibits that the Court has. On the B/C/S version of that document which is immediately following a divider page, it starts on page 13, which has the ERN number of 00798805. What's troubling to the Defence, Your Honour, with respect to the following pages in the B/C/S, on the top left hand corner, it specifically states that it's a copy of a report made by Ramic Jusuf, a copy was made by Swedish police, page 20. The text that we received Friday or Saturday of the original text of that document, does not have - and we have that document here - does not have that description on the top left-hand side of any of these pages. So we really don't know ourselves, Your Honour, and we invite the Prosecutor to help us with that. However, what we were able to do, based on the documents that we did receive, was to find at the Court's request the front page, which is in B/C/S, and there's two signature pages which, for the record, if I may just read their ERN number, the first one being ERN number 00798790, and the second one being 00798792, that we can tender to the Court as requested, with the usher's assistance, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, first, to the Prosecutor. I'm afraid the Prosecutor actually doesn't have these pages. If the witness can help us understanding the language, what it is said -- what is said on the document dated 21 May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the document dated 21st of May, 1992, at the top it says: "the republican staff of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Underneath it says: "Municipal Territorial Defence Prijedor." Then there is a handwritten protocol number. Underneath, it says the 21st of May, 1992. Then it says, "Re: Order on the appointment of Jusuf Ramic." Underneath it says: "Pursuant to the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the decision of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the decree law on the armed forces, Jusuf Ramic is appointed commander of the regional Territorial Defence staff in Puharska. This decision shall enter into force on the day it is issued." At the end it says: "Commander of the Territorial Defence staff Prijedor, Lieutenant-Colonel Muharem Handanagic." And there are seals at the top and at the bottom which say around -- the seal in small letters, it says: "Territorial Defence staff, Bosnia and Herzegovina," and in the middle, it says: "Prijedor Territorial Defence staff."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, do you know this Mr. Muharem Handanagic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's very difficult to work with such a non-document insofar as we have it before us. But I think we shouldn't waste time now. Please proceed with your line of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, with your permission, ask the witness, Mr. Sejmenovic, to read the document as well because I think it relates to the question that the Court posed prior to our break. And it has the ERN number 00798792.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, we would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, directing your attention to the document bearing the ERN number 00798792, would you please read that document out loud for us.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. This is a document which at the top bears the letterhead of the United Nations. Underneath, it says: "UNHCR, Zagreb. The UN High Commissioner for Refugees office in Zagreb." Address: "Kupska Street number 2, Zagreb, Croatia." Then there is a handwritten date, the 2nd of September, 1993. Underneath it says: "To whom it may concern: We hereby certify that" and then the lines are filled in, "Mr. Jusuf Ramic, born on the 15th of October, 1947, registered with the UNHCR under number VV-00081, is under the protection of this office. The certificate shall be valid for one month." On the right-hand side, it says that "The certificate has been extended from the 21st of September, 1993," and it bears the stamp of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees. And then there are two more seals to the right and to the left. On the left-hand side, there is the signature of Mr. Jacques Mouchet, who is in charge of the mission, and on the right-hand side, the same certificate has again been extended, and the extension is certified with a seal. Underneath it says: "Extended until the 22nd of December, 1993" and then there is the signature and an outline of a stamp which is not clearly visible. In the middle on the right-hand side, the photocopy shows that there was a photograph and that there is a stamp, the details of which cannot be seen on the photograph and the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I'd like also to introduce these three documents in addition to what was provisionally identified as D12, as independent exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm afraid we run into several problems when we, for example, read in the -- we even can't call it a summary, speaking about a detailed description of the Hambarine incident on pages, and indicated them. It's a mixtum compositum of several issues, helicopters bringing in weapons for the Serbs, and so on. I think, to work with this document in a responsible way, a prerequisite would be that we have the document in its entirety, and it should be, indeed, translated in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, fine, if the Defence put the document in. They can arrange the translation, but we can't. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No doubt. But from my perspective, yes, to whom it may concern, who is interested in the special parts may provide translation of those parts but then real translation and not work with these excerpts, and then some pages, and we can't really see the link between these excerpts and the pages in B/C/S. Notwithstanding in order to facilitate today's procedure, the Defence may continue now with a line of questions on the basis of some excerpts they want to emphasise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And Your Honour, obviously, with respect to the Defence case, should we proceed in that manner, we would have the relevant documents, despite the fact that it's a numerous document, translated accordingly. We are given, however, a certain number of documents to work with and, therefore, we presented it to the Court. And I would also like to know if we can see the original of that document or if the Court can see it. But my other question relates to what I earlier said. In the copy that we have, it references the Swedish police. In the document in full that we received apparently does not reference - and I'm making that representation and the Court is welcome to examine that - does not reference the Swedish police. So we, quite frankly, are at a loss as to specifically this document, and that's why we're putting certain issues that were only summarised to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To cut a long story short, I would invite the parties to meet on this issue, to provide the original document, and then to decide how to proceed, what has to be translated and whatnot.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I may proceed just with a couple more questions on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us geographically where Crna Dolina is in relation to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. There is the Crna Rijeka or "black river," and then there is the Crna Dolina or "black valley." Whether this is on the mountain of Kozara or on the other side of the mountain, or if it's in the direction of Grmac, that I'm not quite sure of.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar or do you know of any attempts by three sabotage groups to blow up artillery in the Crna Dolina area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is the first time I've heard of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned provocation and incidents. I'd like to ask you about one that we believe occurred on or about May 2nd, 1992, where a Serbian police officer was killed. Are you familiar with an incident that occurred in the Prijedor Municipality wherein a Serbian police officer was killed, and the suspect or the alleged killer escaped and went to Puharska? Are you familiar at all with that event?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that event. It's possible there was some news about this on the radio, but I really don't remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Clarify this for me, sir: Is it your position that a Crisis Staff in Kozarac did not exist, or you don't know whether or not it existed, from April 30th of May of --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, okay. Okay. Sir, there was a Territorial Defence staff. There were people who probably, by analogy, because there was a Crisis Staff in Prijedor, called this body a "Crisis Staff." They refer to it as such.
